Vulcan debuted in January 2024 and has flown three more times since. On two of those missions — its second, in October 2024 , and its fourth, in February of this year — the rocket experienced an issue with one of its solid rocket boosters (SRBs). In both cases, an SRB nozzle burned through and fell off about 30 seconds after launch. Vulcan Centaur overcame the problem on both launches, successfully delivering its payloads to their designated orbits. But the U.S. Space Force was concerned enough that it decided to pause national security launches on Vulcan until ULA addresses the problem. (Vulcan's third and fourth launches were Space Force missions.) ULA has been working hard on that front, and the company is confident that Vulcan is ready to return to flight. "The integrated team has made great strides in improving our understanding of the SRB anomaly that occurred on the previous Vulcan flight and have identified several potential contributors, which have been mitigated through design and process improvements to the nozzle," the company said in an Oct. 28 update . candidates.title: Gama Raises €15M Seed to Boost Europe’s Solar Array Supply Chain
candidates.raw_excerpt: Europe continues to stack the building blocks for a more robust space economy.  Gama, a French startup developing ultra-light deployable solar arrays, announced a €15M seed round yesterday to boost Europe’s solar array supply chain. The round included funds from a mix of European and US VCs, including Transition Ventures, Planet A, Draper Associates, and Manta Ray. The funds will be used to develop a high-volume production facility outside of Paris, France, which will be capable of producing 100 MW of solar arrays annually. The first units—called Wings—are expected to start rolling off the line next year. Gama also plans to hire ~60 employees in engineering roles across mechanical, electrical, and software. The tech: Gama was initially founded to develop solar-sail technology—which uses the Sun’s energy to propel spacecraft into deep space—but the company quickly transitioned into developing solar arrays to solve the ever-present supply-chain headache for other satellite operators. Nearly every spacecraft in orbit relies on solar panels to power its payloads, but solar cells are built by a small number of providers and can often come with lead times as high as a year or more, according to CEO Andrew Nutter. Additionally, as power needs increase, the size of the solar arrays required to run each satellite grows larger, causing them to become floppy—and less effective at gathering sunlight. While traditional solutions involve adding weight to increase rigidity, Gama’s solution uses software—uploaded into customer flight computers—to help point the solar arrays at the Sun, and to solve the floppy-disk problem without additional mass. “Our approach is to make [solar arrays] as thin and light as possible, so you can have more surface area, and you reduce the cost and the mass. Both are designed to be fully and rapidly reusable — a first in the world of orbital spaceflight. The rapidity of Starship's reuse hinges heavily on SpaceX's recovery strategy: Returning both vehicles directly to the launch mount will enable much faster inspection, refurbishment and reflight, the company has said. candidates.title: Italy’s Revolv Space Closes Series A Funding Round
candidates.raw_excerpt: Revolv Space , a new Italian space company, has closed its Series A Funding round worth 5 million euros ($5.6 million). Revolv Space designs and manufactures motion and power generation systems for satellites. The series A funding round was led by Deep Ocean Capital SGR , which joins Revolv’s shareholders through its Deep Blue Ventures and Deep Blue Space Ventures funds. The company announced the funding round, Nov. 11. About two thirds of the capital raised will go toward industrializing the company’s already qualified motion products and increasing their production capacity. Revolv reports its technologies have been validated through both ground testing and in-orbit operation, and have already found commercial demand among international customers. Revolv now aims for efficient, sustainable serial production, so it can deliver at high volume and establish itself as a reliable partner for satellite constellation programs. With this round, Revolv Space has raised a total of 8.6 million euros ($9.6 million) since its founding. The new capital will speed up the industrialization efforts of the company. candidates.title: Satellite snaps rare birds-eye view of the ISS | Space photo of the day for Nov. 12, 2026
candidates.raw_excerpt: A satellite looks down at the International Space Station in orbit. (Image credit: HEO) A commercial satellite has spotted the International Space Station (ISS), giving us a unique view of the orbiting lab from above. What is it? Most of the time, when we see the ISS, it is from down here on Earth or from the viewpoint of the astronauts onboard, peering out the windows at the station's limbs, solar arrays and instruments. But in this snapshot, which was posted on X on Nov. 9 by the Australian company HEO, we can see the station stretched out in all its glory. HEO specializes in using satellites in low Earth orbit to capture images of other spacecraft, though longer-term the company aims to capture observations far out into the solar system. HEO doesn't build the satellites that take these photos; rather, the company's software tasks the spacecraft to image targets as they come into range. This great photo of the ISS from above, for example, was taken by a satellite operated by BlackSky, a Virginia-based company that holds a non-Earth imaging agreement with HEO . So far, HEO and its partners have captured imagery of a variety of spacecraft in orbit, including the ISS, China's Tiangong space station and the European Space Agency's ERS-2 satellite (while it was hurtling back to Earth in 2024). Why is it incredible? While it might seem that satellites are just hovering above Earth, the space station and other spacecraft in LEO are hurtling through space at roughly 17,500 mph (28,160 kph), hundreds of miles above our planet's surface. A snapshot of a satellite from above is therefore far from mundane. Rather, it requires incredible coordination and technical skill; satellite operators must know precisely when their target will present itself, and their equipment must be capable of getting the shot.

candidates.title: NeuralSat Raises €2.9M to Build Orbital Data Relay Network
candidates.raw_excerpt: The Autobahn is coming for in-space data traffic. German startup NeuralSat announced a €2.9M ($3.2M) pre-seed funding round today to develop a 72-sat in-space data relay and processing network, aimed at speeding up the flow of data to and from space. Capnamic Ventures and Bayern Kapital led the round, which included additional participation from ZOHO.VC, Robin Capital, KIEMIS Holding, and Mission E Capital. NeuralSat is also a member of ESA’s Business Incubation Center (ESA BIC) and the NVIDIA Inception Program. Sharing is caring: Unlike other orbital compute startups—namely, those pitching orbital data centers (ODCs) as a replacement for terrestrial ones—NeuralSat is focusing primarily on the data being gathered and distributed in space today. As the number of satellites in orbit increases—with ESA projecting ~100,000 by 2030, up from 10,200 in 2024—the amount of data being gathered is starting to hit bottlenecks on its path to Earth. candidates.title: Nvidia board weighs Jensen Huang's future as CEO
candidates.raw_excerpt:
Nvidia's board of directors is meeting on Wednesday to decide whether to remove co-founder and CEO Jensen Huang, amid uncertainty over the leadership of the world's leading supplier of AI processors, according to the Wall Street Journal.

The meeting follows Nvidia's announcement on November 8 that it had launched an independent investigation into Huang. A committee of independent directors, assisted by outside legal counsel, is overseeing the inquiry. 

Huang co-founded Nvidia in 1993 with Curtis Priem and Chris Malachowsky. Over more than three decades at the helm, he has led the company's transformation from a maker of graphics chips for computer games into the world's leading supplier of AI processors. Nvidia is currently valued at around $4 trillion.

According to the company's fiscal 2026 annual filing, Huang beneficially owns approximately 870.6 million shares, representing 3.58% of Nvidia, valued at about $162.5 billion based on the stock's November 6 closing price. Approximately 800.9 million of those shares, worth about $149.5 billion at the same price, are held through trusts, limited liability companies and a family foundation involving both Huang and his wife, Lori Huang. The couple share trustee, voting or investment responsibilities in several of these arrangements.

No obvious successor has been identified, raising questions about leadership continuity should Huang depart. Nvidia shares fell about 8% in after-hours trading on Wednesday.

(With input from Reuters)

candidates.raw_excerpt: As more information comes out about Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s numerous affairs with high-profile figures in the tech world, calls are mounting for the embattled chief to resign from his post. So far, numerous members of congress from both sides of the aisle have been joined by media figures like Fox Business host Larry Kudlow in calling for Huang to step down from what is arguably one of the most powerful posts in the world right now. Publications like the Economist have also issued blistering editorials calling for his resignation, characterizing Huang as a “brilliant man — and a fool.” The snafu all stems from reporting by the Financial Times , which recently unveiled that one of Huang’s affairs was with the executive of a Singaporean AI company named Alice Huang. Per the FT ’s reporting, anonymous sources in the US intelligence community believe the woman is a spy for the Chinese government — claims that sparked a massive debate around Nvidia’s central position in the world economy. Setting aside the putrid ethics of cheating on your spouse , whether Huang’s mistress was really a Chinese operative remains to be seen. Beyond Huang, this wouldn’t be the first time the AI industry has had a freakout about seductive honeys from foreign lands, a tacitly xenophobic narrative drawn from Cold War pulp novels. And from another point of view, Huang’s ousting may come at the perfect time. Financial markets are experiencing turmoil as fears around a hyperinflated AI bubble become mainstream . If someone in Huang’s position was ever going to get out while the getting is good, it seems now would be the time — though given how topsy-turvy this saga has been already, what the AI chip billionaire does next is anyone’s guess

candidates.raw_excerpt: On Nov. 11, 1966, the Gemini 12 mission launched an astronaut crew into orbit and set the stage for NASA's Apollo program to land humans on the moon. Gemini 12 was the last mission of the Gemini program. It had two astronauts on board: Jim Lovell and Buzz Aldrin . NASA wanted to send humans to the moon. But first, it needed to make sure crews had the right skills, like docking vehicles in space and taking spacewalks. Before Gemini 12, astronauts struggled with spacewalks because there weren't enough handholds on their spacecraft. NASA made some spacewalk changes for Gemini 12. Aldrin performed three spacewalks and spent more than five hours working in space with no major problems. Gemini 12 also successfully docked to an unpiloted Agena booster that launched the same day. The astronauts returned to Earth after four days in space. Both Aldrin and Lovell went on to join the Apollo program . Aldrin became the second person to walk on the moon during Apollo 11 , and Lovell became the commander of Apollo 13 . The Gemini 12 astronauts James Lovell and Edwin Aldrin lifted off aboard a Titan launch vehicle from the Kennedy Space Center on November 11, 1966, an hour and a half after their Agena target vehicle was orbited by an Atlas rocket. (Image credit: NASA/MSFC) Why it mattered Gemini 12 may have closed out NASA's Gemini program of two-person space missions, but it established the mission also established the fundamentals of spacewalking that Apollo astronauts would use when they walked on the moon. It's fitting that Aldrin was the primary spacewalker of the mission. A rookie astronaut (and the first to earn a Ph.D.), Aldrin set a precedent by training for his spacewalk in a neutral buoyancy pool in Maryland to better simulate working in weightlessness. candidates.title: Hubble Space Telescope reveals glittering stars with mysterious origins | Space photo of the day for Nov. 11, 2026
candidates.raw_excerpt: The Hubble Space Telescope has captured a breathtaking view of thousands of stars glittering like cosmic jewels in a dazzling display of blue, gold and orange. But this spectacular scene is far more than just a pretty picture. Some of these stars are almost as old as the universe itself and could hold clues to how our Milky Way formed. M30 is a globular star cluster located approximately 27,500 light-years from Earth. (Image credit: ESA/Hubble & NASA, M. Libralato, G. Piotto, A. Sarajedini) What is it? The exquisite image released by ESA on Nov. 5 shows Messier 30 (M30), a densely packed collection of stars located approximately 27,500 light-years from Earth in the constellation Capricornus. M30 is a globular cluster, a roughly spherical collection of tens of thousands to millions of stars held together by gravity . Our Milky Way is home to at least 150 of these ancient stellar gatherings, some of which are estimated to be between 11.5 billion and 13.5 billion years old. For comparison, the universe itself is approximately 13.8 billion years old! Why is it amazing Besides looking like a vast cosmic treasure trove glittering across the universe, M30 also has a fascinating story to tell. Globular clusters are essentially cosmic time capsules. Their ancient stars preserve chemical clues about the conditions that existed when they formed, helping astronomers piece together the Milky Way's early history. Astronomers have also discovered that M30, along with several other globular clusters, traverses the Milky Way in the opposite direction to the galaxy's rotation. This unusual motion raises the intriguing possibility that M30 may not have formed in our galaxy at all. It could have simply been captured by the Milky Way billions of years ago.
